'''''Akebia quinata''''' –commonly known as {{nihongo|'''''akebi'''''|木通}},<ref name=Nishida>{{Cite book|editor=西田尚道|title =日本の樹木|date=2009|publisher =Gakushūken|series=増補改訂 ベストフィールド図鑑|volume=5|isbn=978-4-05-403844-8|page =12 |language=ja}}</ref><ref name=草木>{{cite book |language=ja |author1=鈴木庸夫 |author2=高橋冬 |author3=安延尚文 |title=『草木の種子と果実』 |publisher=Seibundo Shinkosha |date=2012 |isbn=978-4-416-71219-1 |page=200}}</ref><ref name="gledhill">{{cite book |last=Gledhill |first=David |year=2008 |title=The Names of Plants |publisher=Cambridge University Press |page=40 |isbn=9780521866453}}</ref> '''chocolate vine''', '''five-leaf chocolate vine''',<ref>{{Cite book|url=http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf |title=English Names for Korean Native Plants |publisher=[[Korea National Arboretum]] |year=2015 |isbn=978-89-97450-98-5 |location=Pocheon |page=345 |access-date=25 January 2016 |via=[[Korea Forest Service]] |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20170525105020/http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf |archivedate=25 May 2017 }}</ref> or '''five-leaf akebia'''– is a vine that is native to Japan, China and Korea, commonly used as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]] or [[edible]] plant in the United States and Europe.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Akebia |url=https://onegreenworld.com/product-category/vines/akebia/ |access-date=2023-01-09 |website=One Green World |language=en-US}}</ref> In its native habitat, it is often found on hills, in hedges, on trees, along forest edges and streams, and on mountainous slopes.<ref name=":1" />

== Etymology ==
''Akebi'', its [[Japanese language|Japanese]] vernacular name, was originally written as {{Ruby|開|あ}}け{{Ruby|実|び}}; it derives from {{nihongo3|"to open"|開ける|akeru}} and {{nihongo3|"fruit"|実|mi}}, due to its fruit splitting open when ripe.<ref>{{Cite book |author=田中孝治 |title =効きめと使い方がひと目でわかる 薬草健康法 |language=ja |year=1995 |publisher =[[Kodansha]] |series=ベストライフ |isbn=4-06-195372-9 |pages=121–122 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|editor=平野隆久 |year=1997 |title =樹木ガイドブック|language=ja |publisher =Nagaokashoten |page =241 |isbn=4-522-21557-6 }}</ref>

The epithet ''quinata'' means 'divided into five' and is presumably a reference to its lobed leaves.{{sfn|Gledhill|2008|p=324}}

== Description ==
''Akebia quinata'' is a climbing evergreen vine that grows to {{convert|10|m|ft|-1|abbr=on}} or more in height and has palmately compound leaves with five elliptic or obovate leaflets that are notched at the tip.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Akebia quinata {{!}} chocolate vine/RHS Gardening|url=http://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/747/Akebia-quinata/Details|access-date=2021-04-21|website=www.rhs.org.uk|language=en-gb}}</ref> The woody stems are greyish-brown with [[lenticel]]s.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Thompson|first=John Peter|date=November 22, 2019|title=Akebia quinata (five-leaf akebia)|url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/3933|url-status=live|access-date=April 21, 2021|website=CABI Invasive Species Compendium|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170725183602/http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/3933 |archive-date=2017-07-25 }}</ref>

The flowers are clustered in [[racemes]] and are [[chocolate]]-scented, with three or four [[sepals]]. The fruits are sausage-shaped pods which contain edible pulp.<ref name=Levy-Yamamori>{{cite book|author= Levy-Yamamori, Ran|author2=Ran Levy|author3=Gerard Taaffe | title= Garden Plants of Japan |publisher=Timber Press| year=2004 | isbn=0-88192-650-7|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vTl40WdPNkQC&q=akebia+quinata+japan&pg=PA266|accessdate=2009-04-05}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/25231326#page/209/mode/1up |title=Decaisne, Joseph. Archives du Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle 1: 195, pl. 13a. 1839 |publisher=Biodiversitylibrary.org |date=2013-05-30 |accessdate=2018-05-31}}</ref> The gelatinous [[placentation]] contains seeds surrounded with white pulp that has a sweet flavor.{{Citation needed|date=September 2014}}

==Uses==

=== Culinary ===
The fruit contains a sweet soft pulp, eaten primarily in Japan as a seasonal delicacy. The rind, with a slight bitter taste, is used as vegetable, fried and stuffed with ground meat or mushrooms.<ref>{{cite web |title=Chocolate vine|url=https://www.kew.org/plants/chocolate-vine |access-date=21 November 2025 |website=kew.org |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |language=en}}</ref>

Often eaten fresh, the Akebia fruit is best after it fully opens naturally on the vine.<ref name="cookist.com">{{Cite web |title=Here's Everything You Need To Know Purple Akebi Fruit |url=https://www.cookist.com/heres-everything-you-need-to-know-purple-akebi-fruit/ |access-date=2023-01-09 |website=Cookist.com |language=en}}</ref> The fruiting season is from September to October.<ref name="Nishida"/> The seeds are very bitter and can even lead to throat irritation if chewed. They are discarded by spitting out or simply swallowing them whole. The fruit can be processed into jams, jellies, drinks and even added to smoothies or ice-creams.<ref name="cookist.com"/>

=== Ornamental ===
''Akebia quinata'' is often grown as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]] plant in the United States, Canada, Europe and Asia. It is primarily used to cover less attractive spots on the sides of businesses or a ground cover to prevent [[erosion]] of hills.<ref name=Bailey>{{Cite book |last=Bailey |first=L. H. |author-link=L. H. Bailey |url=http://www.gutenberg.org/etext/9550 |title=Manual of Gardening |date=2005 |publisher=[[Project Gutenberg|Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation]] |edition=Second }}</ref> The flowers bloom generally in April - May<ref name=草木/> and produce a "chocolatey" aroma which is often compared to [[vanilla]] or sometimes [[nutmeg]] rather than chocolate.<ref name=Bailey />

Various breeders of the plant have created new subspecies with their own unique colored flowers. One of these is the "Silver Bells" ''Akebia'' which has silvery white flowers with purple stamen.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Silver Bells ™ Akebia Vine |url=https://onegreenworld.com/product/silver-bells-2/ |access-date=2023-01-10 |website=One Green World |language=en-US}}</ref> (see photo in Gallery)

=== Medicinal ===
''Akebia quinata'' consumption has been shown [[In vitro|in-vitro]] to lower [[cholesterol]] levels present in the blood of rodents.<ref name="Lee 4683">{{Cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Seul Gi |last2=Lee |first2=Eunbi |last3=Chae |first3=Jongbeom |last4=Kim |first4=Jin Soo |last5=Lee |first5=Han-Saem |last6=Lim |first6=Yu-Mi |last7=So |first7=Jai-Hyun |last8=Hahn |first8=Dongyup |last9=Nam |first9=Ju-Ock |date=2022-11-05 |title=Bioconverted Fruit Extract of Akebia Quinata Exhibits Anti-Obesity Effects in High-Fat Diet-Induced Obese Rats |journal=Nutrients |volume=14 |issue=21 |pages=4683 |doi=10.3390/nu14214683 |issn=2072-6643 |pmc=9656223 |pmid=36364945 |doi-access=free }}</ref> ''Akebia'' also has the ability to regulate chemicals in the [[kidney]]s, [[liver]] and [[Circulatory system|cardiovascular system]] making it a health food if regularly consumed.<ref name="Lee 4683"/>

The stem contains approximately 30% [[potassium]] [[salt (chemistry)|salts]] thus causing a [[diuretic]] action.<ref>{{cite book |last=Reid |first=Daniel |year=2001 |title=A Handbook of Chinese Healing Herbs |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |isbn=962-593-988-1}}</ref>{{medrs|date=December 2016}}

The fruit is used in [[traditional Chinese medicine]] to treat urinary tract infections, scanty lactation, and rheumatoid arthritis.

=== Other ===
The dried rinds have been used in Japanese fertility festivals and due to their vulva-like appearance it is thought to increase the fertility of women, although there is no scientific evidence to support these claims.

==Cultivation==
[[File:Akebia in PNW.jpg|thumb|A bunch of ''Akebia'' fruit growing on a vine in western Washington)]]
''Akebia'' prefers sandy soils with good drainage, and regular watering, though it is drought resistant.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gardenia.net/plant/akebia-quinata-chocolate-vine|title=Akebia quinata (Chocolate Vine)| website=Gardenia.net}}</ref> In some areas the plant is an invasive species to be avoided.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://davesgarden.com/guides/pf/go/369|title = PlantFiles: Akebia Species, Chocolate Vine, Five-Leaf Akebia, Raisin Vine| website=Dave's Garden | date=2003-04-15}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=McIntosh | first=Jamie | title=Chocolate-Scented Flowers Make Akebia Vine Unique | website=The Spruce | date=2011-11-23 | url=https://www.thespruce.com/grow-chocolate-vine-1316033}}</ref> This species is considered hardy in all of Europe (down to −15 to −20 °C).<ref name=":0" /> In the US, it suitable for [[hardiness zone]]s 4–9.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Five Leaf Akebia Info|url=https://www.gardeningknowhow.com/ornamental/vines/chocolate-vine/chocolate-vine-plants.htm|url-status=live|access-date=2021-04-21|website=www.gardeningknowhow.com|date=13 May 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130328105352/http://www.gardeningknowhow.com/ornamental/vines/chocolate-vine/chocolate-vine-plants.htm|archive-date=2013-03-28}}</ref>

''Akebia quinata'', and all ''[[Akebia]]'' species for that matter, will only produce fruit if pollinated by a genetically different plant (e.g., male flowers from the mother plant or the male flowers from a [[Cloning|clone]] of the mother plant will not be able to pollinate the female flowers). Two separate varieties or two Akebia grown from separate seeds are needed to produce the sausage-like fruits.<ref>{{Cite report|title=Akebia quinata (five-leaf akebia) |date=2022 |language=en |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.3933 |last1=Thompson |first1=J. P. |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Distribution ==
[[File:Range of Akebia.png|thumb|Range of ''Akebia quinata'' worldwide (only includes reports confirmed by botanists.) Potential numbers may far exceed what is shown in this map.]]

=== Native range ===
''Akebia quinata'' is native to China, Japan (all major islands except [[Hokkaido]]<ref name=草木/>) and the [[Korean peninsula]],<ref>{{cite powo |id=106376-1 |title=''Akebia quinata'' (Thunb. ex Houtt.) Decne.}}</ref> but is cultivated globally.
This map represents sightings of both wild and cultivated plants.

=== In North America ===
''Akebia quinata'' is an [[invasive species]] in the majority of the [[East Coast of the United States|East Coast]] and was introduced in 1845 as an ornamental plant.<ref name="IPA">{{Cite web |title=chocolate vine: Akebia quinata (Ranunculales: Lardizabalaceae): |url=https://www.invasiveplantatlas.org/subject.html?sub=10090 |website=Invasive Plant Atlas of the United States |publisher=[[University of Georgia]] Center for Invasive Species and Ecosystem Health and the National Park Service |access-date=9 January 2023 }}</ref> This is because the plant has no natural predators or diseases in North America and can grow as it pleases. Its shade tolerance and ability to endure full sun allow it to adapt to nearly all conditions it is grown in, and it will smother native shrubs and trees by blocking sunlight.  In the [[East Coast of the United States|East Coast]], ''Akebia quinata'' has been reported in, [[Florida]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], [[Alabama]], [[Louisiana]], [[Tennessee]], [[South Carolina]], [[North Carolina]], [[Missouri]], [[Kentucky]], [[Virginia]], [[West Virginia]], [[Ohio]], [[Indiana]], [[Illinois]], [[Delaware]], [[Maryland]], [[Pennsylvania]], [[New Jersey]], [[New York (state)|New York]], [[Massachusetts]], [[Vermont]], [[Connecticut]], [[Rhode Island]], and as far north as [[Michigan]] and [[Wisconsin]].<ref name="IPA"/>  On the [[West Coast of the United States|west coast]], it has been reported in the states of [[Washington (state)|Washington]] and [[Oregon]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Holscher |first=Mary |date=13 October 2019  |url=https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/34310298 |title=Five-leaf Akebia (Akebia quinata) |language=en |website=iNaturalist |access-date=9 January 2023 }}</ref>
